A.explanation: Same frequency alone is not enough, as the phase difference could still drift randomly and prevent stable fringes.

B.explanation: Coherent waves have the same frequency and a phase difference that does not change with time, giving a stable interference pattern.

C.explanation: Equal intensity affects fringe contrast but is not part of the definition of coherence.

D.explanation: Zero phase difference is only one special case of constant phase difference, so it is too restrictive.

hints: Notice the question links coherent waves to the appearance of stable interference fringes from two light sources.
Recall that a fixed fringe position needs a fixed path-difference to phase-difference relationship, so the phase difference between the sources must not drift with time.
Compare constant phase difference with the stricter idea of zero phase difference and with same frequency or same intensity alone.
walkthrough: Identify the situation: two light sources overlap and a stable pattern of bright and dark interference fringes is observed.
State the physical rule: for stable constructive and destructive superposition, the two waves must have the same frequency $f$ and a phase difference $\phi$ that is constant in time.
Explain why: if the phase difference varied randomly, the positions of constructive and destructive interference would move rapidly and the fringes would wash out.
Check the options: same frequency alone and same intensity alone do not guarantee a fixed phase relationship, and zero phase difference is only one possible constant value.
Therefore the definition that captures coherence is emission with constant phase difference. This is option B.
